package_info.package_name: Emotet, AZORULT, Lokibot, Grandoreiro, Agent Tesla, FormBook, HawkEye
package_info.package_manager: malspam/email delivery (not a software package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: These malware families are distributed via COVID-19-themed malspam campaigns, leveraging social engineering to deceive users into opening malicious attachments or clicking links. The delivered payloads perform credential theft, keylogging, banking fraud, and other malicious actions by exploiting document macros, abusing file icons, or delivering executables disguised as legitimate files. The attack chain results in unauthorized access to sensitive data and financial accounts.

execution_context.trigger: user opens attached Word document and enables macros

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: VBA macro embedded in Word document that downloads and executes Emotet payload
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the attached Word document and enables macros, the VBA macro executes, downloads the Emotet malware from a remote server via HTTP/HTTPS, writes the payload to disk, and launches it as a new process, resulting in Emotet execution on the victim's machine.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Macros in unsolicited documents that initiate network connections to download and execute code are a well-known malware delivery technique, especially for Emotet.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Word documents should not contain macros that download and execute external binaries; macros are typically used for document automation, not code execution from the internet.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise workflows use macros for automation, but never to download and run untrusted executables from the internet.
key_indicators: Network request to remote server for executable download

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious macro or exploit code in Word document exploiting MS Office vulnerabilities to install AZORULT
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the malicious Word document, embedded macro or exploit code executes, exploiting Office vulnerabilities to escalate privileges or bypass security, downloads the AZORULT infostealer, writes it to disk, and executes it, leading to credential and sensitive data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Office documents exploiting vulnerabilities or containing macros that install infostealers like AZORULT are highly suspicious and indicative of targeted attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate documents do not exploit software vulnerabilities or install additional software, especially infostealers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for exploiting Office vulnerabilities or installing infostealers via document macros.
key_indicators: Macro-initiated download and execution of infostealer

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Executable or script in attachment that installs Lokibot
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the malicious attachment, the executable or script runs, installs Lokibot on the system, accesses stored credentials and sensitive information, and exfiltrates the data to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unexpected executables or scripts in email attachments are a common vector for malware like Lokibot, especially when disguised as documents.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate business emails do not send executables disguised as documents or scripts that install credential-stealing malware.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: No legitimate business process involves sending credential-stealing executables as attachments.
key_indicators: Executable or script disguised as document
Process creation from email client or document viewer

execution_context.trigger: user clicks malicious link in email

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Malicious link downloads Grandoreiro banking trojan executable
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user clicks the malicious link in the email, the browser downloads a Grandoreiro banking trojan executable, which the user may then execute, resulting in credential theft, banking fraud, and exfiltration of sensitive financial data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Links in emails that directly download executables, especially banking trojans like Grandoreiro, are highly suspicious and rarely used in legitimate communication.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate organizations do not send links to direct executable downloads in unsolicited emails, particularly for banking-related software.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software vendors may send download links, but never for banking trojans or in unsolicited emails.
key_indicators: Direct download of executable from email link
Banking trojan payload with credential theft capabilities
Unusual download activity following email link click

execution_context.file_location: email attachment (executable disguised as Excel file)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Agent Tesla keylogger executable with Excel file icon
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user opens the email attachment, which appears as an Excel file but is actually a PE executable, the Agent Tesla keylogger is installed, captures keystrokes and clipboard data, and exfiltrates this information to attacker-controlled servers.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Executables disguised as documents using icons and double extensions are a classic malware trick, commonly used by Agent Tesla.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Excel files are not PE executables and do not perform keylogging or data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate reason for an executable to masquerade as a document in business communication.

execution_context.trigger: user opens ZIP archive and runs contained executable

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Executable in ZIP archive launches GuLoader, which installs FormBook infostealer
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user extracts and runs the executable from the ZIP archive, GuLoader executes, downloads the FormBook infostealer from a remote server, installs it, and FormBook then steals credentials and exfiltrates them to the attacker's infrastructure.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: ZIP archives containing a single executable, especially loaders like GuLoader, are a common method for delivering infostealers such as FormBook.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate ZIP archives from trusted sources rarely contain only a loader for infostealer malware.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Software distribution may use ZIPs, but not for infostealer loaders or without clear provenance.
key_indicators: ZIP archive with single PE executable
Subsequent infostealer installation and data exfiltration

execution_context.trigger: user opens email attachment or clicks link

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: HawkEye infostealer payload delivered via phishing email
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user interacts with the email attachment or clicks the link, the HawkEye infostealer payload is executed, collects credentials and sensitive information, and exfiltrates the data to attacker-controlled servers.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Infostealer payloads like HawkEye delivered via phishing emails are a hallmark of malspam campaigns and are never legitimate.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate emails do not deliver or execute infostealer payloads under any circumstances.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for infostealer delivery via email.
key_indicators: Infostealer payload in email attachment or link

attack_chain.action: User receives COVID-19-themed phishing email with malicious attachment or link.
attack_chain.leads_to: User opens attachment or clicks link.

attack_chain.action: User opens malicious document, executable, or link, triggering embedded code or download.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code executes on victim's machine.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code downloads and installs malware payload (Emotet, AZORULT, Lokibot, Grandoreiro, Agent Tesla, FormBook, HawkEye).
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware executes and begins data theft or other malicious activity.

attack_chain.action: Malware exfiltrates credentials, keystrokes, or banking information to attacker-controlled servers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains access to sensitive information or financial accounts.

behavioral_signatures: Office documents with macros that initiate network connections and download executables
Executables or scripts disguised as documents (e.g., using Excel or Word icons, double extensions like .doc.exe)
ZIP archives containing a single PE executable, especially loaders like GuLoader
Unexpected outbound network connections immediately after opening email attachments or links
Process creation of infostealer or keylogger binaries (e.g., Agent Tesla, FormBook, HawkEye) following document or attachment open
file_indicators: Word documents with embedded auto-executing macros
Email attachments with double extensions (e.g., invoice.doc.exe)
ZIP archives with only one executable file inside
PE executables with document-style icons (e.g., Excel, Word)
Attachments or downloads with filenames mimicking legitimate documents but are actually executables
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known C2 infrastructure for Emotet, AZORULT, Lokibot, Grandoreiro, Agent Tesla, FormBook, HawkEye
Unusual HTTP/HTTPS POST requests to suspicious or newly registered domains after opening attachments
Connections to IPs/domains associated with malware delivery or exfiltration as identified in threat intelligence feeds
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor email gateways for COVID-19-themed phishing emails containing attachments or links. Flag Office documents with macros, especially those that initiate network connections or drop executables. Detect executables masquerading as documents by analyzing file headers, extensions, and icons. Alert on ZIP archives containing only a single executable. Monitor endpoint behavior for process creation from email clients or document viewers, particularly if followed by network activity to suspicious domains. Use threat intelligence to block or alert on known C2 domains and IPs associated with these malware families. Correlate user actions (e.g., opening attachments) with subsequent network and process activity to identify suspicious chains.
